sections.b: Jeremiah's collection (46-51 in the Hebrew) runs through Egypt, Philistia, Moab, Ammon, Edom, Damascus, Kedar and Hazor, Elam, and ends with Babylon. The Greek moves the whole collection to the middle of the book (after 25:13) and arranges it differently (Elam, Egypt, Babylon, the Philistines, Edom, Ammon, Kedar, Damascus, Moab). The Hebrew has about a seventh more, including four promises that nations will be restored (Egypt 46:26, Moab 48:47, Ammon 49:6, Elam 49:39), of which the Greek lacks three. Chapter 48 reuses Isaiah 15-16, and 49:7-22 overlaps Obadiah.

Jeremiah 46 has two poems on Egypt. The first dates from 605 BC and the defeat of Pharaoh Neco's army by Nebuchadnezzar at Carchemish; the second foretells a Babylonian invasion of Egypt, naming Migdol, Memphis and Tahpanhes, the same towns where Judean refugees lived (44:1). The prophet mocks Pharaoh as 'all noise' and promises that Egypt will be inhabited again (46:26). Jeremiah himself went to Egypt after Gedaliah's murder (43:6-7).

Nebuchadnezzar is named in the nations oracles as the victor at Carchemish (46:2), the coming invader of Egypt (46:13, 26), and the plotter against Hazor (49:28-30). The Babylonian Chronicle supports the first; for the second, a Babylonian fragment of his thirty-seventh year (568/567 BC) tells of a clash with Egypt but is broken, and the Chronicle also reports a raid on the Arabs in 599/598 BC.

Jeremiah 47 pictures a flood from the north over the Philistine coast: Gaza bald, Ashkelon silent, the island of Caphtor's remnant cut off. The LORD's sword has orders against Ashkelon. The Babylonian Chronicle reports that Nebuchadnezzar took Ashkelon in Kislev 604 BC, and excavations found its burned layer.

Jeremiah 48 is the longest nations oracle. It names more than twenty places in Moab, reuses Isaiah 15-16 and the old song of Numbers 21:28-29, pictures Moab as wine left on its dregs, and says Chemosh will go into exile. It charges Moab with pride and trust in its own works. The prophet weeps for Moab, and the chapter ends with a promise to turn Moab's fortunes around in the last days (48:47).

Heshbon, Sihon's old city, is named in Jeremiah 48:2, 34, 45 and 49:3. Jeremiah 48:45-46 reuses the old song from Numbers 21:28-29: the fire that once went out from Heshbon for Sihon now burns against Moab.

Jeremiah 48:35 says the LORD will end the one who offers on the high place and burns incense to his gods in Moab. King Mesha's stone says he made a high place for Chemosh. Solomon's high place for Chemosh was destroyed by Josiah (2 Kings 23:13).

Jeremiah 48:11-12 uses winemaking as a picture of national pride: wine left on its dregs keeps its taste and smell, because it was never poured out; the LORD will send men to tip the jars. The verse is a close relative of Zephaniah 1:12, where complacent Jerusalemites are 'settled on their dregs'.

sections.h: 'Cursed is he who keeps his sword from blood'
sections.b: Jeremiah 48:10 pronounces a curse on the one who does the LORD's work in a lazy way or holds his sword back from blood. It is addressed to the instrument of judgment against Moab, the Babylonian army. It sits with the holy war texts in 1 Samuel 15 and 1 Kings 20:42 and has been used since to justify violence, a use the verse does not itself make.
In Jeremiah 48:31-36 the speaker howls and cries for Moab, and says 'my heart throbs like flutes'. Isaiah 16:9-11 has the same grief. Scholars disagree whether the grief is real or ironic.

Jeremiah 49:1-6 accuses Ammon's god Milcom of taking over Gad's land and promises that Israel will take back what was taken. Rabbah will become a mound of ruins, Milcom will go into exile with his priests and officials, and in the end Ammon's fortunes will be turned around. King Baalis of Ammon appears in 40:14 and 41:10.

Jeremiah 49:7-22 mocks the wisdom of Teman, promises that the cliffs will not save Edom, and shows God stripping Esau bare. It shares text with Obadiah 1-9. Verse 11 offers shelter to Edom's orphans and widows. Bozrah, Edom's chief city, is to be a ruin; like Sodom, no one will live there.
The short oracle at Jeremiah 49:23-27 shows Hamath, Arpad and Damascus losing heart at bad news, and fire in the wall of Damascus eating the citadels of Ben-hadad. Its language resembles Amos 1:3-5.

Jeremiah 49:28-33 sends Nebuchadnezzar against Kedar, the Arab tribe descended from Ishmael's son, and against the 'kingdoms of Hazor', Arab settlements. Their tents, flocks and camels are carried off; those who cut the hair at their temples are scattered to every wind. The Babylonian Chronicle reports a raid on the Arabs in 599/598 BC.
The 'kingdoms of Hazor' in Jeremiah 49:28-33 are not the great northern city. The word means an enclosure or settled camp, and the oracle uses it of an Arab area. The Greek takes it as 'court'.

sections.h: The cup in the nations oracles
sections.b: The cup of the LORD's anger (25:15-29) turns up in the nations oracles: Moab is made drunk and flops in its own vomit (48:26), and Edom is told that even those not sentenced to drink must drink, and it will not go unpunished (49:12). Revelation 14:10 uses the picture again.

sections.h: Promises of restoration to the nations
sections.b: Four oracles in Jeremiah 46-49 end with a promise: Egypt will be inhabited again (46:26), and the fortunes of Moab (48:47), Ammon (49:6) and Elam (49:39) will be turned around. They are 'in the last days' for Moab and Elam. The Greek lacks the first three. 46:27-28 also repeats the promise to Jacob in 30:10-11.

The last oracle breaks the bow of Elam, scatters its people to the four winds and sets the LORD's throne in Elam, but in the last days the LORD will turn Elam's fortunes around (49:34-39). It is dated early in Zedekiah's reign, 597/596 BC.
Jeremiah 46:2 dates the defeat of Pharaoh Neco's army at Carchemish to the fourth year of Jehoiakim (605 BC). The Babylonian Chronicle records the same battle.
Jeremiah 47:4 says the Philistines' last helpers will be cut off from Tyre and Sidon, their trading partners. Tyre and Sidon are also in the cup list of 25:22 and the conspiracy of 27:3.

sections.h: Sodom as the model of ruin
sections.b: Edom (Jeremiah 49:18) and Babylon (50:40) are to end like Sodom and Gomorrah and their neighbor towns, with no one living there.
